opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because people love a single number. They want to know "how much energy does AI use?" as if AI were one thing. But when we actually started measuring different models across different tasks, what really jumped out was how enormous the spread is depending on what you're asking the model to do.

Take something like text classification, where the model looks at a sentence and decides whether it's positive or negative. The output is basically a label. Now compare that to image generation, where you're producing a whole new image pixel by pixel, often through many denoising steps. Those aren't remotely the same amount of computation, so of course the energy is going to differ by orders of magnitude. If you line them up side by side and say "this model is a thousand times less efficient than that one," you're not really comparing efficiency. You're comparing two completely different jobs.

It's a bit like comparing the fuel consumption of a scooter and a moving truck. The truck uses way more fuel, but it's also doing something the scooter can't do. The meaningful question is: given the task you actually need done, which truck or which scooter does it most efficiently?

So the comparisons that matter are within a task. If I need summarization, how do the different summarization models compare? And there you still see really big differences, sometimes from model size, sometimes from architecture, sometimes just from deployment choices like batching or the hardware it's running on. That's where you can make informed decisions.

The other piece is that cross-task comparisons can hide the bigger issue, which is the trend of using huge general-purpose generative models for everything. If you use a giant multipurpose model to do something a small task-specific classifier could do, you might be spending many times more energy for basically the same result. That's the real efficiency story, and it gets lost if we just rank everything on one big leaderboard without context.

So what I always push for is apples-to-apples: same task, same data, same hardware setup, and then compare. And be transparent about it, because right now a lot of the companies deploying these models don't disclose this kind of information at all, which makes it really hard for users to make good choices.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts positive/negative text classification with image generation and says their energy use differs by orders of magnitude because image generation requires much more computation, communicating that sentiment analysis is far less energy-intensive.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something that came out of the work we did on measuring the energy consumption of inference across a bunch of different tasks, and I think the core issue is that when people say "AI energy use," they're treating it as if it's one thing, and it really isn't. The variance across tasks is enormous. We looked at things like text classification, question answering, summarization, image classification, and then image generation, and the gap between the cheapest and the most expensive tasks was literally orders of magnitude. Generating a single image with some of the diffusion models we tested used about as much energy as charging your phone, whereas classifying a piece of text used a tiny fraction of that.

So if you take an average, or you make a general statement like "AI uses X amount of energy per query," you're basically washing out all of that information. And the thing is, the differences aren't just about the task, they're also about the modality, the model size, and especially whether you're using a general-purpose model or a task-specific one. One of our findings was that using a big multi-purpose generative model to do something like sentiment analysis can cost tens of times more energy than a small model that was fine-tuned specifically for that. So the "same" task can have wildly different footprints depending on how you choose to do it.

And then there's the question of what you're even measuring. Energy per query? Energy per token? Energy per useful output? For a classification task the output is one label, for a generative task it might be a paragraph or an image, so even the unit of comparison isn't obvious. If you compare them naively you end up penalizing or rewarding models for things that have nothing to do with how efficient they actually are.

What I think is more useful is to compare like with like, so models doing the same task on the same hardware with the same setup, and to be really transparent about the methodology. That way a practitioner can actually look and say, okay, for my use case, this architecture is more efficient than that one. The headline number comparisons across totally different tasks make for good tweets, but they don't really help anyone make better decisions, and they can even be misleading in ways that let people either dismiss the problem or overstate it.

r001.rationale: The response compares image generation with text classification and compares two model choices for sentiment analysis, but never states that sentiment analysis uses far less energy than image generation.

astra-6.text:
Because you’re not necessarily comparing the same amount of work. Classifying a piece of text and generating an image are very different tasks, with different computational requirements. So if one uses more energy, that doesn’t automatically mean it’s less efficient—it’s doing something different.

The more useful comparison is between systems that can accomplish the same task, at a similar level of quality. Then you can ask: how much energy does each one need to get that result? And do you actually need a general-purpose generative model, or could a smaller, specialized model meet your needs with less energy?

r001.rationale: The response contrasts text classification with image generation but does not state that sentiment analysis uses far less energy; it only says the tasks have different computational requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
Because you’re comparing systems that are doing fundamentally different things. Classifying a piece of text into one of a few categories isn’t the same task as generating a paragraph, and neither is the same as generating an image. The outputs are different, and so is the computation required to produce them. So an energy number on its own doesn’t tell you whether a model is efficient.

What’s more useful is to hold the task constant: for a particular application, how much energy do different models use to achieve a comparable level of performance? That also lets you ask whether you need a general-purpose generative model at all, or whether a smaller, specialized model can do the job with much less energy.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts text classification with image generation but never identifies sentiment analysis or states that it uses far less energy than image generation.
